Hoorn
horn
n. (port of North Holland on the Zuiderzee; a town of the revolt from 1572 and a base of the fleet that won the Zuiderzee)
Dutch Hoorn, a horn, from the hook or spit of land on which the harbour was built; the town gave its name to Cape Horn through its merchants.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Hoorn was one of the great ports of North Holland, rich on the Baltic trade, the herring fishery and later on the East India traffic, and it went over to the prince of Orange in the summer of 1572 with Enkhuizen and the other Zuiderzee towns. Its ships were in the squadron which beat the Spanish fleet on the Zuiderzee in October 1573 and took its admiral, an action which secured the northern quarter of Holland for the revolt and is rightly ranked with the land defences of Haarlem and Alkmaar. Hoorn's Reformed congregation was established at once, and the town afterwards had a Latin school and a vigorous consistory. It also had, as a trading port, the ordinary problem of such places: a church whose leading members were merchants in a town whose prosperity came to depend on a company trading in slaves and on wars fought in the East Indies, and a consistory which had to decide how much of that it would examine. The dictionary enters Hoorn because the question is a real one and has never gone away. A congregation of prosperous traders must either apply the law of God to the trade or be an ornament of it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines commerce as an interchange of goods between nations; a company as an association of persons for a joint concern; and covetousness as an inordinate desire of gain.

expand to see more

COMMERCE, n. An interchange or mutual change of goods, wares or merchandise between nations or individuals; trade; traffick.

COMPANY, n. An association of persons for the purpose of carrying on some commercial or industrial undertaking.

COVETOUSNESS, n. A strong or inordinate desire of obtaining and possessing some supposed good; an eagerness for gain.

FISHERY, n. The business of catching fish; a place for catching fish with nets or hooks.

CONSISTORY, n. An assembly of ecclesiastical persons for the regulation of church affairs; a church court.

1Ti 6:10 — "For the love of money is the root of all evil: which while some coveted after, they have erred from the faith, and pierced themselves through with many sorrows."

Jam 5:4 — "Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth: and the cries of them which have reaped are entered into the ears of the Lord of sabaoth."

Mal 2:7 — "For the priest's lips should keep knowledge, and they should seek the law at his mouth: for he is the messenger of the LORD of hosts."

Modern Corruption

North Holland port of the revolt from 1572, whose fleet won the Zuiderzee, and whose consistory had to judge the trade its members lived by.

expand to see more

The corruption to be named is the church that will not examine the business of its own leading men. The Dutch ports grew rich in the seventeenth century on commerce which included the traffic in slaves and the armed monopoly of the Indies, and the consistories of those towns were composed in large part of the men who held the shares. “For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10) is not a text about the poor, and “Behold, the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud, crieth” (Jam 5:4) is addressed to employers by name.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the discipline of a church must reach the men who pay for it. A consistory which disciplines a servant for drunkenness and cannot ask a director how his cargo was obtained has not got discipline at all; it has a police for the poor. “the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7) includes the knowledge of what the law of God says about a trade, and the courage to say it where it will cost the collection.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek philarguria (G5365), the love of money; Greek misthos (G3408), wages, hire.

expand to see more

Greek philarguria (G5365) — the love of silver, covetousness; “the love of money is the root of all evil”, 1 Timothy 6:10.

Greek misthos (G3408) — wages, hire, reward; “the hire of the labourers”, James 5:4.

Greek apostereo (G650) — to defraud, to keep back; “which is of you kept back by fraud”, James 5:4.

Hebrew da'ath (H1847) — knowledge; “the priest's lips should keep knowledge”, Malachi 2:7.

Greek antilego (G483) — to speak against, to gainsay; “to convince the gainsayers”, Titus 1:9.

Usage

"“For the love of money is the root of all evil” (1Ti 6:10) — a consistory of merchants in a town that lived by trade."

"“the hire of the labourers who have reaped down your fields, which is of you kept back by fraud” (Jam 5:4) — addressed to employers by name."

"“the priest's lips should keep knowledge” (Mal 2:7) — and the courage to say it where it will cost the collection."
